'''Richard "Dick" E. Norberg''' was a professor of physics at [[Washington University in St. Louis]]. His research focused on nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR).

== Biography ==
Norberg grew up in [[Evanston, Illinois]], studied at [[DePauw University]], and earned his bachelor's degree in absentia in 1943 while serving in the [[United States Air Force]] in [[World War II]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.depauw.edu/academics/departments-programs/physics-astronomy/alumni/list-of-majors/|title=List of Majors|website=DePauw University|language=en|access-date=2019-12-29}}</ref> After returning in 1946, he received his master's and doctoral degrees in physics from the [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign|University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign]] in 1947 and 1951, respectively, as the first Ph.D. student of [[Charles Pence Slichter|Charles Slichter]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/photos/norberg-richard-c2|title=Dick Norberg (left) converses with Bill Slichter Norberg Richard C2|date=2014-02-24|website=www.aip.org|language=en|access-date=2019-12-29}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Slichter|first=Charles P.|date=2012-07-01|title=In Memory of Albert W. Overhauser (1925–2011)|journal=Applied Magnetic Resonance|language=en|volume=43|issue=1|pages=3–6|doi=10.1007/s00723-012-0339-4|issn=1613-7507|doi-access=free}}</ref> He joined the physics department at Washington University in St. Louis in 1954 to work for [[George Pake]]. He was quickly hired as a professor, and served as department chair from 1962–1991.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Conradi|first1=Mark S.|last2=Leopold|first2=Daniel J.|last3=Friedlander|first3=Michael W.|date=2010-12-01|title=Richard E. Norberg|journal=Physics Today|volume=63|issue=12|pages=76–77|doi=10.1063/1.3529011|issn=0031-9228|bibcode=2010PhT....63l..76C|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/pake-george.pdf|title=Biographical Memoir of George Pake|last=Slichter|first=Charles|date=|website=National Academy of Sciences|access-date=}}</ref> He retired in 1993 from teaching and worked part-time until 2003. Over the course of his career he advised 47 Ph.D. students.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://source.wustl.edu/2010/04/richard-e-norberg-pioneering-nmr-physicist-dies-at-87/|title=Richard E. Norberg, pioneering NMR physicist, dies at 87 {{!}} The Source {{!}} Washington University in St. Louis|date=2010-04-21|website=The Source|language=en-US|access-date=2019-12-29}}</ref>  He made many contributions to NMR.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.weizmann.ac.il/ISMAR/richard-e-norberg-irving-j-lowe|title=Richard E. Norberg & Irving J. Lowe {{!}} ISMAR|website=www.weizmann.ac.il|access-date=2019-12-29}}</ref>

He was married and had three children.

== Awards ==

* Fellow, [[American Physical Society]], 1957<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/units/dqi/fellowship/index.cfm?initial=&year=&unit_id=APS&institution=|title=APS Fellows|last=|first=|date=|website=American Physical Society|access-date=}}</ref>
* [[Alfred P. Sloan Fellowship|Alfred P. Sloan Fellow]], 1955-1957<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://source.wustl.edu/2010/04/richard-e-norberg-pioneering-nmr-physicist-dies-at-87/|title=Richard E. Norberg, pioneering NMR physicist, dies at 87 {{!}} The Source {{!}} Washington University in St. Louis|date=2010-04-21|website=The Source|language=en-US|access-date=2019-12-29}}</ref>
* ISMAR Prize from [[International Society of Magnetic Resonance in Medicine|International Society of Magnetic Resonance]], 2004<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://source.wustl.edu/2004/10/norberg-shares-prestigious-ismar-prize/|title=Norberg shares prestigious ISMAR Prize {{!}} The Source {{!}} Washington University in St. Louis|date=2004-10-21|website=The Source|language=en-US|access-date=2019-12-29}}</ref>
